newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Chinese cotton exports seen unlikely near-term.
newsitem.headline: Chinese cotton exports seen unlikely near-term.

text.p: The huge differential between high domestic Chinese cotton prices and lower international prices means China is unlikely to export near-tern despite mammoth stocks, traders said on Monday.
Domestic cotton prices are currently around 18,000 yuan (US$2,168) a tonne, roughly equivalent to 98 U.S. cents a pound, while world prices are closer to 73 cents a lb.
China was forecast to hold nearly half of world stocks at the end of 1996/97, according to an International Cotton Advisory Committee (ICAC) report issued on Monday.
If China choses to export that cotton, then world prices could drop dramatically, the ICAC said.
But one Hong Kong-based cotton analyst said China might want the world to believe it could launch huge exports to main pressure on prices, because import demand remains despite the high inventories.
He estimated Chinese stocks at between seven to eight million bales.
One Chinese mill was reported to be looking for cotton towards the lower end of the market's current 70-90 U.S. cents a lb trading range, traders said.
"The price of cotton depends on the southern hemisphere's crop and how much Australia produces," one source said.
The Australian Bureau of Agriculture and Resource Economics (ABARE) last month reduced its forecast of Australia's 1996/97 (July-June) record cotton harvest to 2.43 million bales or 552,000 tonnes.

China's farmers are currently forming their cotton planting decisions for this year, traders said, adding that estimates for the country's 1997 production would only emerge after the planting season ended.
"At this time of year, nobody can tell you what is going on in China, simply because the planting for the (new) cotton crop has not started," said one cotton trader in Hong Kong.
China has set a cotton production target of 4.25 million tonnes in 1997, minister of the State Planning Commission Chen Jihua told the National People's Congress on Sunday.
The area under cultivation would be increased to 534,000 hectares (1.32 million acres), Chen said, but gave no further details.
Traders said, however, the real issue was how willing individual provinces and farmers were to obey state directives.
"Nobody can tell what the farmers think and what the intentions are of each individual cotton producing province," another cotton source noted.
Farmers are preparing the land for planting and for cotton favourable weather conditions are crucial, with planting impossible if conditions are too wet or too dry.
Most of China's cotton planting takes place in April, and sometimes extends into May with some southern provinces starting earlier in March if the weather permits.
"If farmers (miss) the planting period, they will have to plant other crops instead," one analyst said.
Cotton and grain prices will heavily influence farmers' crop planting decisions, traders said.
"State procurement prices for grain on the whole are higher than for cotton," a Western industry source said.
-- Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843 6358
